metadata.narrative: I'm trying to scope out my research proposal. It's focused on decentralized control for a heterogeneous swarm (UAVs and UGVs) doing search and rescue in unstructured, GPS-denied environments. Think collapsed buildings, dense forests, etc First, I need a way for each agent to handle its own state estimation. I'm thinking multi-sensor fusion, that is, fusing onboard vision, LiDAR, and IMU data for robust SLAM and odometry, but it also has to be good enough to detect survivors or hazards, not just navigate. How do we manage real-time role assignment, eg who's mapping, who's actively searching, who's clearing debris? It needs to be decentralized and robust to failures. for example if a drone battery dies or a ground bot gets stuck, the system has to autonomously reallocate its tasks without a central coordinator. The comms will be spotty, so how does the swarm propagate critical info like victim locations, new hazards, blocked passages, etc over an ad-hoc mesh network that's constantly dropping connections? Maybe some distributed mapping or data sharing protocol? For the analysis, I need to show this framework is actually effective. We probably need some formal or at least strong empirical guarantees? Something to show that, say 90% of reachable victims are located within a bounded time, even if we lose up to 30% of the agents. Finally, for evaluation, I'm planning to implement this in a high-fidelity simulator, probably ROS/Gazebo, with realistic sensor noise and complex terrain. Then I'd run it across maybe three disaster scenarios of increasing complexity. We'd need to report metrics on coverage, victim-finding rate, rescue latency, and the network overhead to make sure it's efficient.

answer.text: Decentralized control for a heterogeneous UAV-UGV swarm doing search and rescue in collapsed buildings and forests needs to be scoped around five coupled subsystems: per-agent state estimation that also senses victims and hazards, real-time decentralized role assignment, failure-tolerant task reallocation, an intermittent ad-hoc mesh for critical-information sharing, and a simulation-based evaluation plan with quantitative guarantees.

For per-agent state estimation, a proven building block is extended-Kalman-filter fusion of an IMU, a monocular camera, and a 2D LiDAR to produce full 3D pose estimates for a UAV in an unknown GPS-denied environment, validated in both simulation and real flight tests.

This kind of fusion generalizes to ground platforms too, since legged locomotion frameworks for quadrupeds such as HyQ combine perception-driven foothold planning, whole-body torque control, and disturbance observers to traverse debris, ramps, and stairs, directly relevant to a UGV clearing role in rubble.

The same onboard sensor suite used for SLAM can double as a detection pipeline: autonomous mine-rescue aerial robots fuse LiDAR, thermal vision, and inertial cues for GPS-denied localization and mapping while a deep-learning classifier searches the reconstructed volumetric map for survivors and associated objects such as backpacks or phones.

A complementary, non-vision detection layer combining CO2/O2 gas sensors, a microphone with SVM-based voice-activity detection, and a thermal camera successfully localized a simulated buried casualty in eight of nine trials within about one hour in a high-fidelity collapsed-building test site, giving a concrete multi-modal victim-detection metric.

DARPA's Subterranean Challenge showed that heterogeneous robot teams operating without GPS or reliable communications could still generate maps differing from expert ground truth by under one percent in under an hour, evidence that fused multi-sensor autonomy scales to kilometer-length unstructured environments.

For decentralized role assignment, a minimal-communication approach lets robots switch between roles such as mapping, searching, or clearing purely through probabilistic transitions triggered by local encounters with other robots, converging to a desired task distribution without any explicit messaging.

The Consensus-Based Bundle Algorithm and its Partial-Replanning extension provide a decentralized, peer-to-peer auction that provably converges to a near-optimal, conflict-free allocation in O(nt times D) communication rounds and can absorb newly discovered tasks, such as a fresh hazard report, without a full team-wide re-solve.

A collision-aware auction variant adds a proven fifty-percent optimality lower bound while discouraging robots from being assigned overlapping paths, which matters when UAVs and UGVs share a corridor inside a collapsed structure.

Because consensus-based allocation is itself message-intensive, a communication-aware extension learns which agents should transmit or stay silent based on local network density, improving convergence specifically in ad-hoc, bandwidth-constrained environments like the one this proposal targets.

When agents are lost or degraded rather than merely delayed, a resilient task-allocation framework reoptimizes robot-to-task assignments based on measured capability degradation, producing graceful performance loss instead of catastrophic failure.

More broadly, resilient multi-robot coordination under robot failure is formally NP-hard, but bounded approximation algorithms built on robust submodular optimization and network reconfiguration can still guarantee a fraction of optimal reward while restoring team connectivity after losses.

A real heterogeneous deployment validating this division-of-labor idea is the Emesent-CSIRO Data61-Georgia Tech SubT team, which fielded drones, tracked crawlers, and quadrupeds that explored autonomously while sharing local map data over a self-formed wireless mesh network, with Georgia Tech supplying the coordination and division-of-labor framework across the fleet.

For propagating victim locations, hazards, and blocked passages over a dropping mesh, Kimera-Multi, MIT's distributed multi-robot SLAM system, lets robots exchange map data with semantic annotations whenever they come within communications range, incrementally building one globally consistent map without any central server.

DiSCo-SLAM achieves a similar goal more cheaply by fusing lidar and inertial odometry on each robot and exchanging only lightweight scan-context descriptors at rendezvous points, keeping bandwidth use low even for large 3D point-cloud maps.

At the protocol layer, teams in DARPA's Subterranean Challenge learned to drop battery-powered mesh-network nodes like breadcrumbs as robots advanced, restoring connectivity after early tunnel-circuit tests in which robots lost contact after the first bend.

Purpose-built disaster routing such as Disaster-Optimized Spray-and-Wait, a delay-tolerant-network protocol, prioritizes high-urgency messages so victim and hazard alerts are delivered with higher probability while keeping the overhead ratio roughly constant despite intermittent connectivity.

Quantitatively, comparisons of AODV, BCHP, and DSDV mobile ad-hoc routing protocols show that control-message overhead can consume thirty to sixty percent of total throughput, with cluster-based BCHP giving the best overhead-to-reliability tradeoff, a useful baseline for reporting network overhead in the proposed evaluation.

For the effectiveness analysis, the strongest available empirical precedent is a decentralized, behavior-based UAV swarm that located over ninety percent of survivors in under one hour in disaster-realistic simulations while continuing to operate through individual robot failures or crashes, closely matching the target ninety-percent-within-bounded-time metric.

A related evaluation pattern deliberately disables robots mid-mission to observe how a distributed mapping colony degrades, a directly applicable methodology for stress-testing coverage and victim-finding rate under a thirty-percent agent-loss condition.

For a more formal treatment, probabilistic real-time schedulability analysis offers a template for bounding the probability that a mission deadline is missed, comparing a probabilistic worst-case response-time distribution against an acceptable failure-probability threshold rather than a hard worst case.

Combining this schedulability-style threshold argument with the bounded-approximation guarantees for resilient coordination under failures gives a plausible formal backbone for a claim like ninety percent of reachable victims within bounded time under thirty percent agent attrition, though the committed evidence does not include a single paper proving that exact joint bound, which remains an identified gap for further analytical or simulation work.

Finally, for the ROS/Gazebo evaluation plan, the RoboCup Rescue Simulation League's Virtual Robot Competition is a ready-made, peer-validated benchmark built on ROS/Gazebo with heterogeneous ground and air robots, standard sensors and actuators, and established mapping, exploration, and navigation tasks, making it a strong template for constructing three increasing-complexity disaster scenarios and reporting coverage, victim-finding rate, rescue latency, and network overhead.

# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

For per-agent state estimation, a proven building block is extended-Kalman-filter fusion of an IMU, a monocular camera, and a 2D LiDAR to produce full 3D pose estimates for a single UAV in an unknown GPS-denied environment, validated in both simulation and real flight tests. [00508_44376]
This kind of fusion generalizes to ground platforms too, since legged locomotion frameworks for quadrupeds such as HyQ combine perception-driven foothold planning, whole-body torque control, and disturbance observers to traverse debris, ramps, and stairs, which is directly relevant to a UGV role in rubble. [00150_74098]
Critically, the same onboard sensor suite used for SLAM can double as a detection pipeline: autonomous mine-rescue aerial robots fuse LiDAR, thermal vision, and inertial cues for GPS-denied localization and mapping while a deep-learning classifier searches the reconstructed volumetric map for survivors and associated objects such as backpacks or phones. [01548_68906]
At the system level, DARPA's Subterranean Challenge showed that heterogeneous robot teams operating without GPS or reliable communications could still generate maps differing from expert ground truth by under one percent in under an hour, evidence that fused multi-sensor autonomy scales to kilometer-length unstructured environments. [02399_20431]

For decentralized role assignment, several mechanisms avoid any central coordinator while remaining formally analyzable.
A minimal-communication approach lets robots switch between roles such as mapping, searching, or clearing purely through probabilistic transitions triggered by local encounters with other robots, converging to a desired task distribution without any explicit messaging. [00563_70316]
The Consensus-Based Bundle Algorithm and its Partial-Replanning extension provide a decentralized, peer-to-peer auction that provably converges to a near-optimal, conflict-free allocation in O(nt·D) communication rounds and can absorb newly discovered tasks, like a fresh hazard report, without a full team-wide re-solve. [01135_37566]
A collision-aware auction variant adds a proven fifty-percent optimality lower bound while explicitly discouraging robots from being assigned overlapping paths, which matters when UAVs and UGVs share the same corridor of a collapsed structure. [04197_13192]
Because CBBA-style consensus is itself message-intensive, a communication-aware extension learns which agents should transmit or stay silent based on local network density, improving convergence specifically in communication-constrained, ad-hoc environments like the one this proposal targets. [01476_21025]
When agents are lost or degraded rather than merely delayed, a resilient task-allocation framework reoptimizes robot-to-task assignments based on measured capability degradation, exhibiting graceful performance loss rather than catastrophic failure. [02654_73087]
More broadly, resilient multi-robot coordination under robot failure is formally NP-hard, but bounded approximation algorithms built on robust submodular optimization and network reconfiguration can still guarantee a fraction of optimal reward while restoring team connectivity after losses. [03811_73292]
A real heterogeneous deployment validating this division-of-labor idea is the Emesent–CSIRO Data61–Georgia Tech SubT team, which fielded drones, tracked crawlers, and quadrupeds that explored autonomously while sharing local map data over a self-formed wireless mesh network, with Georgia Tech supplying the coordination and division-of-labor framework across the fleet. [03994_56216]
